canonical_statement: This Review summarizes current evidence regarding the pathogenesis, epidemiology, diagnosis, and management of classic Hodgkin lymphoma in adults aged 18 years and older.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: This Review summarizes current evidence regarding the pathogenesis, epidemiology, diagnosis, and management of cHL in adults aged 18 years and older.

canonical_statement: The authors searched PubMed for English-language articles related to classic Hodgkin lymphoma published from January 1, 2010, through April 23, 2026.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: We performed a PubMed search for English-language articles related to cHL published from January 1, 2010, to April 23, 2026

canonical_statement: The PubMed search used the query ("Hodgkin Disease"[Majr] OR hodgkin*[ti]) and excluded case reports, letters, editorials, and animal studies.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: ("Hodgkin Disease"[Majr] OR hodgkin*[ti]), excluding case reports, letters, editorials, and animal studies.

canonical_statement: The search retrieved 5145 articles; the authors also reviewed NCCN and ESMO guidelines and identified additional articles from references, including publications before 2010.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: This search retrieved 5145 articles. We also reviewed guidelines from the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) and European Society for Medical Oncology.

canonical_statement: The Review included 125 articles: 69 observational studies, 37 clinical trials, 9 narrative reviews, 4 systematic reviews or meta-analyses, and 6 guideline recommendations.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: This Review includes 125 articles, composed of 69 observational studies, 37 clinical trials, 9 narrative reviews, 4 systematic reviews or meta-analyses, and 6 guideline recommendations.

canonical_statement: The review describes the malignant cell in classic Hodgkin lymphoma as the Reed-Sternberg cell derived from germinal-center B lymphocytes.
Reed-Sternberg cells in classic Hodgkin lymphoma lack normal B-cell receptor expression and rely on dysregulated NF-kB, JAK-STAT, and PI3K-AKT signaling to avoid apoptosis.
Reed-Sternberg cells constitute less than 2% of classic Hodgkin lymphoma tumor volume and are surrounded by an extensive inflammatory infiltrate.
The review describes chromosome 9p24.1 and PD-L1 locus copy-number changes with increased PD-L1 expression as a mechanism that supports immune evasion in classic Hodgkin lymphoma.
Classic Hodgkin lymphoma accounts for approximately 90% to 95% of Hodgkin lymphoma cases.
Classic Hodgkin lymphoma has a bimodal age distribution, with a first peak at 15 to 35 years and a smaller peak around age 70 years; the median age at diagnosis is 33 years.

The review identifies familial predisposition, Epstein-Barr virus infection, immune-mediated disorders, immunosuppression, and some immunosuppressive therapies as risk factors associated with classic Hodgkin lymphoma.
The review reports that first-degree relatives of patients with Hodgkin lymphoma had a standardized incidence ratio of 3.3 for Hodgkin lymphoma in a European cohort.

population.label: First-degree relatives of 13,922 patients with Hodgkin lymphoma

canonical_statement: The review reports a relative risk of 4.0 for Epstein-Barr virus–positive classic Hodgkin lymphoma after Epstein-Barr virus infection in a Danish and Swedish cohort.

population.label: Danish and Swedish patients evaluated after Epstein-Barr virus infection

canonical_statement: The review reports a standardized incidence ratio of 2.0 for Hodgkin lymphoma among Swedish patients with immune-mediated diseases.
The review reports that people with HIV/AIDS had a standardized incidence ratio of 11.03 for Hodgkin lymphoma in a meta-analysis of 7 cohorts.

population.label: People with HIV/AIDS across 7 cohort studies

canonical_statement: The review reports that transplant recipients had a standardized incidence ratio of 3.89 for Hodgkin lymphoma in a meta-analysis of 4 cohorts.

The review reports a hazard ratio of 12.1 for Hodgkin lymphoma with combined thiopurine and anti–tumor necrosis factor therapy versus no exposure to these therapies in an inflammatory bowel disease cohort.

concept.text: Thiopurine plus anti–tumor necrosis factor therapy
Neither thiopurine nor anti–tumor necrosis factor therapy

canonical_statement: The 2022 WHO classification recognizes 4 histologic subtypes of classic Hodgkin lymphoma: nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte rich, and lymphocyte depleted.
In the United States, the review reports that approximately 75% of classic Hodgkin lymphoma is nodular sclerosis, 20% mixed cellularity, 5% lymphocyte rich, and less than 1% lymphocyte depleted.

Circulating tumor DNA–based molecular clusters of classic Hodgkin lymphoma have not been incorporated into consensus guidelines because classification schemes are heterogeneous and sequencing access is not universal.
Most patients with classic Hodgkin lymphoma present with painless supradiaphragmatic lymphadenopathy involving cervical, mediastinal, supraclavicular, or axillary lymph nodes.

Approximately 30% to 40% of patients with classic Hodgkin lymphoma have B symptoms: fever above 38.3 °C, drenching sweats, or unintentional weight loss above 10% of body weight over the preceding 6 months.
Diagnosis of classic Hodgkin lymphoma requires identification of Reed-Sternberg cells within a polymorphous inflammatory infiltrate in a biopsy specimen.

Excisional lymph node biopsy is preferred over core needle biopsy for suspected classic Hodgkin lymphoma because Reed-Sternberg cells are scarce and tissue architecture is important for histologic subtype identification.
Reed-Sternberg cells typically express CD30 and CD15, show weak PAX5 expression, and lack CD19, CD20, CD79a, and CD45 on immunohistochemistry.
Classic Hodgkin lymphoma is staged anatomically using the Lugano classification with FDG-PET/CT.

Routine bone marrow evaluation is generally not required for classic Hodgkin lymphoma staging because early-stage marrow involvement is uncommon and FDG-PET/CT is highly sensitive for bone involvement.
The review reports a SEER distribution of 15% stage I, 41% stage II, 23% stage III, and 21% stage IV among 10,912 patients with Hodgkin lymphoma.
Early-stage classic Hodgkin lymphoma is classified as favorable or unfavorable according to high-risk features used by NCCN, EORTC, and GHSG risk-stratification systems.

Risk factors used across early-stage classic Hodgkin lymphoma systems include older age, B symptoms, bulky disease, greater number of nodal sites, extranodal involvement, and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate.

The review describes disease bulk as a nodal mass greater than 10 cm or a mediastinal mass greater than one-third of the internal transverse thoracic diameter at T5-T6 on chest radiograph in commonly used risk systems.
Guideline-recommended treatment for early-stage classic Hodgkin lymphoma is chemotherapy with or without consolidative radiotherapy.

For early-stage classic Hodgkin lymphoma, combined chemotherapy and radiotherapy generally improves progression-free survival relative to chemotherapy alone, while overall survival is similar because salvage therapy can be effective after relapse.

The decision to use radiotherapy in early-stage classic Hodgkin lymphoma should consider age, comorbidities, disease location, and long-term risks such as secondary malignancy and cardiopulmonary dysfunction.
An interim FDG-PET/CT after approximately 2 treatment cycles is used to support response-adapted de-escalation in early-stage classic Hodgkin lymphoma.
Patients with favorable early-stage classic Hodgkin lymphoma are treated with ABVD chemotherapy, typically 2 or 4 cycles, with or without consolidative radiotherapy.

exposures.details: Typically 2 or 4 cycles, with or without consolidative radiotherapy

canonical_statement: The review reports that in EORTC/LYSA/FIL H10F, PET-negative favorable early-stage patients had 10-year progression-free survival of 85.4% with ABVD alone versus 98.8% with ABVD plus radiotherapy.

population.label: PET-negative favorable early-stage classic Hodgkin lymphoma

canonical_statement: The review reports that in PET-negative patients in the RATHL trial, 7-year progression-free survival was 81.0% with continued ABVD and 79.2% after bleomycin omission with AVD, with a hazard ratio of 1.10.
For PET-negative early-stage patients, omission of radiotherapy can be considered when reducing long-term radiation-related morbidity outweighs a modestly higher relapse risk.
Patients with unfavorable early-stage classic Hodgkin lymphoma can receive chemotherapy-only strategies or combined-modality therapy using chemotherapy or novel agents plus radiotherapy.
Guideline-included combined-modality options for early-stage unfavorable classic Hodgkin lymphoma include brentuximab vedotin–AVD plus radiotherapy and concurrent nivolumab-AVD plus radiotherapy.

concept.text: Brentuximab vedotin–AVD plus radiotherapy or concurrent nivolumab-AVD plus radiotherapy

canonical_statement: Current guideline-recommended treatment for advanced-stage classic Hodgkin lymphoma is chemotherapy combined with novel agents.
The review identifies nivolumab-AVD for 6 cycles as the preferred regimen in the United States for stage III-IV classic Hodgkin lymphoma.

The review reports that SWOG S1826 showed 3-year progression-free survival of 91% with nivolumab-AVD versus 82% with brentuximab vedotin–AVD in advanced-stage classic Hodgkin lymphoma, with a hazard ratio of 0.48.
The review reports 3-year overall survival of 98% with nivolumab-AVD and 97% with brentuximab vedotin–AVD in SWOG S1826.

For patients ineligible for immunotherapy because of autoimmune disease or comorbidities requiring active immunosuppression, guideline options include brentuximab vedotin–containing regimens such as BrECADD or brentuximab vedotin–AVD.

The review reports that ECHELON-1 showed 6-year progression-free survival of 82.3% with brentuximab vedotin–AVD versus 74.5% with ABVD in stage III-IV classic Hodgkin lymphoma, with a hazard ratio of 0.68.
The review reports that ECHELON-1 showed 6-year overall survival of 93.9% with brentuximab vedotin–AVD versus 89.4% with ABVD in stage III-IV classic Hodgkin lymphoma, with a hazard ratio of 0.59.
Suspected relapsed or refractory classic Hodgkin lymphoma should be re-biopsied to confirm persistent or recurrent disease.
Approximately 10% to 15% of patients with classic Hodgkin lymphoma develop relapsed or refractory disease, with most relapses occurring within 2 years of first-line therapy.
Guideline-recommended care for transplant-eligible relapsed or refractory classic Hodgkin lymphoma is salvage therapy followed by high-dose chemotherapy and autologous stem cell rescue.

population.label: Transplant-eligible relapsed or refractory classic Hodgkin lymphoma

concept.text: Salvage therapy followed by high-dose chemotherapy and autologous stem cell rescue

canonical_statement: No salvage regimen for relapsed or refractory classic Hodgkin lymphoma has been established as superior through randomized head-to-head trials.

The review reports that a retrospective cohort of 1280 patients with relapsed or refractory classic Hodgkin lymphoma had 2-year progression-free survival of 88.2% after immunotherapy-based salvage, 70.2% after brentuximab vedotin–based salvage, and 67.4% after chemotherapy-only salvage before autologous transplant.

population.label: Patients with relapsed or refractory classic Hodgkin lymphoma treated from 2010-2022

canonical_statement: After autologous stem cell transplant, guidelines recommend considering brentuximab vedotin maintenance for high-risk patients who have not previously received brentuximab vedotin.

population.label: High-risk post-autologous transplant classic Hodgkin lymphoma without prior brentuximab vedotin

canonical_statement: The review reports that AETHERA showed 5-year progression-free survival of 59% with post-transplant brentuximab vedotin versus 41% with placebo in high-risk relapsed or refractory classic Hodgkin lymphoma, with a hazard ratio of 0.52.

population.label: High-risk relapsed or refractory classic Hodgkin lymphoma after autologous stem cell transplant

canonical_statement: Allogeneic stem cell transplant is generally reserved for eligible patients who relapse after autologous stem cell transplant.
For patients ineligible for autologous stem cell transplant, treatment is individualized according to disease extent and comorbidities and is generally palliative rather than curative.

The review estimates overall survival above 97% for early-stage favorable disease, above 95% for early-stage unfavorable disease, and above 90% for advanced-stage classic Hodgkin lymphoma in clinical trials with at least 2 years of follow-up.

After autologous stem cell transplant for relapsed or refractory classic Hodgkin lymphoma, the review summarizes progression-free survival above 75% to 80% and overall survival above 90% across multiple studies.

Routine post-treatment surveillance imaging is not recommended in asymptomatic classic Hodgkin lymphoma survivors because survival benefit has not been demonstrated; imaging and laboratory testing should be clinically indicated.
The review reports a standardized incidence ratio of 4.6 for second cancers among 3905 Hodgkin lymphoma survivors who had survived at least 5 years after treatment initiation.

population.label: Hodgkin lymphoma survivors alive at least 5 years after treatment initiation

canonical_statement: Secondary malignancies are the leading cause of death among classic Hodgkin lymphoma survivors, with notable risks including non-Hodgkin lymphoma and breast, lung, colorectal, skin, and thyroid cancers as well as myelodysplasia.
Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of noncancer-related death among classic Hodgkin lymphoma survivors, and excess risk emerges 5 to 10 years after treatment and persists throughout life.
The review reports a standardized incidence ratio of 6.8 for heart failure among 2524 Hodgkin lymphoma survivors with a median follow-up of 20 years.

population.label: Hodgkin lymphoma survivors with median 20-year follow-up

canonical_statement: The review reports a hazard ratio of 2.91 for pulmonary disease in a Danish cohort of 1474 patients with classic Hodgkin lymphoma compared with age-matched controls.

population.label: Danish patients with classic Hodgkin lymphoma

canonical_statement: Fertility preservation should be discussed before treatment, particularly when alkylating agents, pelvic irradiation, or autologous stem cell transplant are planned.
The review identifies circulating tumor DNA as an emerging method for minimal residual disease detection in classic Hodgkin lymphoma.

Secondary analyses cited in the review suggest that persistent detectable circulating tumor DNA is prognostic for relapse and may be more sensitive than conventional FDG-PET/CT for relapse prediction.

Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy is investigational for relapsed or refractory classic Hodgkin lymphoma and was not approved or commercially available for this indication at the time of the review.
The authors acknowledge that some relevant studies may have been missed.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: First, some relevant studies may have been missed.

canonical_statement: The authors did not perform a systematic evaluation of the quality of evidence included in the Review.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Second, a systematic evaluation of the quality of evidence was not performed.

canonical_statement: The Review excludes management of children and young adolescents younger than 18 years because pediatric risk stratification and chemotherapy regimens differ from adult care.
The authors conclude that first-line treatment for classic Hodgkin lymphoma is chemotherapy, with radiotherapy added for some early-stage patients.

The authors conclude that select patients with unfavorable early-stage disease and all patients with advanced-stage disease should receive anti–PD-1 immunotherapy or a CD30-targeted antibody-drug conjugate in addition to chemotherapy.
The authors conclude that patients with relapsed or refractory classic Hodgkin lymphoma should be evaluated for stem cell transplant.
The authors conclude that cure is achieved in up to 90% of treated patients with early-stage and advanced-stage classic Hodgkin lymphoma.

The article reports that Alison J. Moskowitz received grants and honoraria from multiple pharmaceutical companies during the conduct of the study and additional grants outside the submitted work; no other disclosures were reported.
